claims.text: The as-synthesized Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles are initially homogeneous solid solutions.
The baseline particles have a uniform distribution of all five elements at room temperature.
Copper is the lower-melting-point component of the alloy.
Premelting is initiated by preferential segregation of copper to the nanoparticle surface.
Increasing temperature causes copper atoms to diffuse toward the nanoparticle surface.
A copper-rich surface composition gradient develops before complete melting.
Copper surface segregation lowers the effective local melting temperature.
The locally reduced melting temperature produces a liquid-like surface layer before bulk melting.
The liquid-like premelted region eventually propagates into the particle bulk.
Copper-enriched surfaces will disorder and melt before the particle core.
The particle will retain a solid core until temperatures above the onset of surface premelting are reached.
Reducing copper mobility will delay the onset of premelting relative to the baseline particles.
Partial substitution of copper with a higher-melting-point element can serve as a comparison that reduces copper's influence.
The proposed mechanism primarily applies to nanoparticles smaller than approximately 50 nm, where the surface-to-volume ratio is high.
The proposed mechanism is limited to conditions in which oxidation and extrinsic surface effects are minimized.
The proposed mechanism may not extend to bulk material or to processing conditions that substantially alter atomic mobility.
Strain, configurational entropy, and kinetic effects may make secondary contributions to premelting.
Failure to observe copper enrichment before melting, or failure of a copper-mobility modification to shift premelting onset, would falsify the hypothesis.
